text: III Method

The goal of our framework is to learn with multiple auxiliary tasks to improve the performance of the primary task. In this work, we demonstrate the benefits of our framework with various auxiliary tasks. Especially, we evaluate meta-path prediction as auxiliary tasks. The meta-paths capture diverse and meaningful relations between nodes on heterogeneous graphs [53]. However, learning with auxiliary tasks for graphs has multiple challenges: identifying useful auxiliary tasks, balancing the auxiliary tasks with the primary task, and converting challenging auxiliary tasks into solvable (and relevant) tasks. To address the challenges, we propose SELf-supervised Auxiliary LeaRning (SELAR).
Our framework consists of two main components:
We propose a novel framework that learns weight functions to softly select auxiliary tasks and balance them with the primary task via meta-learning.
We introduce Hint Networks to convert challenging auxiliary tasks into more relevant and solvable tasks to the primary task learner.
III-A Meta-path Prediction as a self-supervised task

Most existing graph neural networks have been studied focusing on homogeneous graphs that have a single type of nodes and edges. However, in real-world applications, heterogeneous graphs [54], which have multiple types of nodes and edges, commonly occur. Learning models on the heterogeneous graphs requires different considerations to effectively represent their node and edge heterogeneity.

Heterogeneous graph. Let [TeX: G=(V,E)] be a graph with a set of nodes [TeX: V] and edges [TeX: E] . A heterogeneous graph [55] is a graph equipped with a node type mapping function [TeX: f_{v}:V\rightarrow\mathcal{T}^{v}] and an edge type mapping function [TeX: f_{e}:E\rightarrow\mathcal{T}^{e}] , where [TeX: \mathcal{T}^{v}] is a set of node types and [TeX: \mathcal{T}^{e}] is a set of edge types. Each node [TeX: v_{i}\in V] (and edge [TeX: e_{ij}\in E] resp.) has one node type, i.e., [TeX: f_{v}(v_{i})\in\mathcal{T}^{v}] , (and one edge type [TeX: f_{e}(e_{ij})\in\mathcal{T}^{e}] resp.). In this paper, we consider the heterogeneous graphs with [TeX: |\mathcal{T}^{e}|>1] or [TeX: |\mathcal{T}^{v}|>1] . When [TeX: |\mathcal{T}^{e}|=1] and [TeX: |\mathcal{T}^{v}|=1] , it becomes a homogeneous graph.

Meta-Path. Meta-path [53, 56] is a path on a heterogeneous graph [TeX: G] that a sequence of nodes connected with heterogeneous edges, i.e., [TeX: {v}_{1}\xrightarrow{t_{1}}{v}_{2}\xrightarrow{t_{2}}\ldots\xrightarrow{t_{l}}{v}_{l+1}] , where [TeX: t_{l}\in\mathcal{T}^{e}] denotes an [TeX: l] -th edge type of the meta-path. The meta-path can be viewed as a composite relation [TeX: R=t_{1}\circ t_{2}\ldots\circ t_{l}] between node [TeX: {v}_{1}] and [TeX: {v}_{l+1}] , where [TeX: R_{1}\circ R_{2}] denotes the composition of relation [TeX: R_{1}] and [TeX: R_{2}] . The definition of meta-path generalizes multi-hop connections and is shown to be useful to analyze heterogeneous graphs. For instance, in Book-Crossing dataset, ‘user-item-written.series-item-user’ indicates that a meta-path that connects users who like the same book series.

We introduce meta-path prediction as a self-supervised auxiliary task to improve the representational power of graph neural networks. To our knowledge, the meta-path prediction has not been studied in the context of self-supervised learning for graph neural networks in the literature.

Meta-path prediction. Meta-path prediction is similar to link prediction but meta-paths allow heterogeneous composite relations. The meta-path prediction can be achieved in the same manner as link prediction. If two nodes [TeX: u] and [TeX: v] are connected by a meta-path [TeX: p] with the heterogeneous edges [TeX: (t_{1},t_{2},\ldots t_{\ell})] , then [TeX: y_{u,v}^{p}=1] , otherwise [TeX: y_{u,v}^{p}=0] . The labels can be generated from a heterogeneous graph without any manual labeling. They can be obtained by [TeX: A_{p}=A_{t_{l}}\ldots A_{t_{2}}A_{t_{1}}] , where [TeX: A_{t}] is the adjacency matrix of edge type [TeX: t] . The binarized value at [TeX: (u,v)] in [TeX: A_{p}] indicates whether [TeX: u] and [TeX: v] are connected with the meta-path [TeX: p] . In this paper, we use meta-path prediction as a self-supervised auxiliary task.

Let [TeX: \mathbf{X}\in\textbf{R}^{|V|\times d}] and [TeX: \mathbf{Z}\in\textbf{R}^{|V|\times d^{\prime}}] be input features and their hidden representations learnt by GNN [TeX: f] , i.e., [TeX: \mathbf{Z}=f(\mathbf{X};\mathbf{w},\mathbf{A})] , where [TeX: \mathbf{w}] is the parameter for [TeX: f] , and [TeX: \mathbf{A}\in\textbf{R}^{|V|\times|V|}] is the adjacency matrix. Then link prediction and meta-path prediction are obtained by a simple operation as
[TeX: \displaystyle\hat{y}_{u,v}^{t}=\sigma(\Phi_{t}(z_{u})^{\top}\Phi_{t}(z_{v})),] (1)

where [TeX: \Phi_{t}] is the task-specific network for task [TeX: t\in\mathcal{T}] and [TeX: z_{u}] and [TeX: z_{v}] are the node embeddings of node [TeX: u] and [TeX: v] . e.g., [TeX: \Phi_{0}] (and [TeX: \Phi_{1}] resp.) for link prediction (and the first type of meta-path prediction resp.).

The architecture is shown in Fig. 1 for link prediction, especially meta-path prediction as auxiliary tasks. To optimize the model, as the link prediction and the meta-path prediction, cross entropy is used. The graph neural network [TeX: f] is shared by the link prediction and meta-path prediction and there is a task-specific function [TeX: \Phi] for each task. As any auxiliary learning methods, the auxiliary task samples (meta-paths) should be carefully chosen and properly weighted so that the auxiliary task (meta-path prediction) does not compete with link prediction (primary task) especially when the capacity of GNNs is limited. To address these issues, we propose our framework that automatically selects meta-paths and balances them with the primary task via meta-learning.
III-B Self-Supervised Auxiliary Learning
Our framework SELAR is learning to learn a primary task with multiple auxiliary tasks to assist the primary task. This can be formally written as

[TeX: \displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{w},\Theta}\;\;\underset{(x,y)\sim D^{pr}\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;}{\text{\large$\mathbb{E}$}\;\;\left[\;\mathcal{L}^{pr}(\mathbf{w}^{\ast}(\Theta))\;\right]}] [TeX: \displaystyle\text{ s.t. }\;\;\mathbf{w}^{\ast}(\Theta)=\argmin_{\mathbf{w}}\underset{(x,y)\sim D^{pr+au}\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;}{\;\;\mathbb{E}\;\;\left[\;\mathcal{L}^{pr+au}(\mathbf{w};\Theta)\;\right]},] (2)

where [TeX: \mathcal{L}^{pr}(\cdot)] is the primary task loss function to evaluate the trained model [TeX: f(x;\mathbf{w}^{\ast}(\Theta))] on meta-data (a validation for meta-learning [41]) [TeX: D^{pr}] and [TeX: \mathcal{L}^{pr+au}] is the loss function to train a model on training data [TeX: D^{pr+au}] with the primary and auxiliary tasks. To avoid cluttered notation, [TeX: f] , [TeX: x] , and [TeX: y] are omitted. Each task [TeX: \mathcal{T}_{t}] has [TeX: N_{t}] samples and [TeX: \mathcal{T}_{0}] and [TeX: \{\mathcal{T}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}] denote the primary and auxiliary tasks respectively. The proposed formulation in Eq. (2) learns how to assist the primary task by optimizing [TeX: \Theta] via meta-learning. The nested optimization problem given [TeX: \Theta] is a regular training with properly adjusted loss functions to balance the primary and auxiliary tasks. The formulation can be more specifically written as

[TeX: \displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{w},\Theta}] [TeX: \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{M}\frac{1}{M}\ell^{0}(y_{i}^{(0,meta)},f(x_{i}^{(0,meta)};\mathbf{w}^{\ast}(\Theta)))] (3) s.t. [TeX: \displaystyle\mathbf{w}^{\ast}(\Theta)=\argmin_{\mathbf{w}}\sum_{t=0}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{t}}\frac{1}{N_{t}}\mathcal{V}(\cdot;\Theta)\ell^{t}(y_{i},\hat{y}_{i}),] (4)

where [TeX: \ell^{t}] and [TeX: f^{t}] denote the loss function and the model for task [TeX: t] . We overload [TeX: \ell^{t}] with its function value, i.e., [TeX: \ell^{t}=\ell^{t}(y_{i},\hat{y}_{i})] where [TeX: \hat{y}_{i}=f^{t}(x_{i}^{(t,train)};\mathbf{w})] . The embedding vector of [TeX: i_{th}] sample for task [TeX: t] denotes [TeX: \xi^{(t,train)}_{i}] . The input of the weighting function is [TeX: \xi^{t}_{i}] . i.e., [TeX: \mathcal{V}(\xi^{t}_{i};\Theta)] . In our experiment, [TeX: \xi^{t}_{i}] is the concatenation of the loss value, one-hot representation of task types, and the label of the sample (positive/negative), i.e., [TeX: \xi^{t}_{i}=\left[\ell^{t};e_{t};y_{i}^{(t,train)}\right]\in\textbf{R}^{T+2}] .
Algorithm 1 Self-supervised Auxiliary Learning

Input: training data for primary/auxiliary tasks [TeX: D^{pr}/D^{au}] , mini-batch size [TeX: N_{pr},N_{au}] Input: max iterations [TeX: K] , # folds for cross validation [TeX: C] Output: network parameter [TeX: \mathbf{w}^{K}] for the primary task
1: for [TeX: k=1] to [TeX: K] do
2: [TeX: D^{pr}_{m}\leftarrow\text{MiniBatchSampler}(D^{pr},N_{pr})]
3: [TeX: D^{au}_{m}\leftarrow\text{MiniBatchSampler}(D^{au},N_{au})]
4: for [TeX: c=1] to [TeX: C] do [TeX: \triangleright] Cross Validation
5: [TeX: D^{pr(train)}_{m},D^{pr(meta)}_{m}\leftarrow\text{CVSplit}(D^{pr}_{m},c)]
6: [TeX: \hat{\mathbf{w}}^{k}(\Theta)\leftarrow\mathbf{w}^{k}-\alpha\nabla_{\mathbf{w}}\mathcal{L}^{pr+au}(\mathbf{w}^{k};\Theta)]
7: with [TeX: D^{pr(train)}_{m}\cup D^{au}_{m}] [TeX: \triangleright] Eq. (6)
8: [TeX: g_{c}\leftarrow\nabla_{\Theta}\mathcal{L}^{pr}(\hat{\mathbf{w}}^{k})] with [TeX: D^{pr(meta)}_{m}] [TeX: \triangleright] Eq. (7)
9: end for
10: Update [TeX: \Theta^{k+1}\leftarrow\Theta^{k}-\beta\sum_{c}^{C}g_{c}] [TeX: \triangleright] Eq.(9)
11: [TeX: \mathbf{w}^{k+1}=\mathbf{w}^{k}-\alpha\nabla_{\mathbf{w}}\mathcal{L}^{pr+au}(\mathbf{w}^{k};\Theta^{k+1})]
12: with [TeX: D^{pr}_{m}\cup D^{au}_{m}] [TeX: \triangleright] Eq. (8)
13: end for

To derive our learning algorithm, we first shorten the objective function in Eq. (3) and Eq. (4) as [TeX: \mathcal{L}^{pr}(\mathbf{w}^{\ast}(\Theta))] and [TeX: \mathcal{L}^{pr+au}(\mathbf{w};\Theta)] . This is equivalent to Eq. (2) without expectation. Then, our formulation is given as
[TeX: \min_{\mathbf{w},\Theta}\mathcal{L}^{pr}(\mathbf{w}^{\ast}(\Theta))\;\;\text{ s.t. }\mathbf{w}^{\ast}(\Theta)=\argmin_{\mathbf{w}}\mathcal{L}^{pr+au}(\mathbf{w};\Theta),] (5)

To circumvent the difficulty of the bi-level optimization, as previous works [19, 41] in meta-learning we approximate it with the updated parameters [TeX: \hat{\mathbf{w}}] using the gradient descent update as
[TeX: \displaystyle\mathbf{w}^{\ast}(\Theta)\approx\hat{\mathbf{w}}^{k}(\Theta^{k})=\mathbf{w}^{k}-\alpha\nabla_{\mathbf{w}}\mathcal{L}^{pr+au}(\mathbf{w}^{k};\Theta^{k}),] (6)

where [TeX: \alpha] is the learning rate for [TeX: \mathbf{w}] . We do not numerically evaluate [TeX: \hat{\mathbf{w}}^{k}(\Theta)] instead we plug the computational graph of [TeX: \hat{\mathbf{w}}^{k}] in [TeX: \mathcal{L}^{pr}(\mathbf{w}^{\ast}(\Theta))] to optimize [TeX: \Theta] . Let [TeX: \nabla_{\Theta}\mathcal{L}^{pr}(\mathbf{w}^{\ast}(\Theta^{k}))] be the gradient evaluated at [TeX: \Theta^{k}] . Then updating parameters [TeX: \Theta] is given as
[TeX: \displaystyle\Theta^{k+1}=\Theta^{k}-\beta\nabla_{\Theta}\mathcal{L}^{pr}(\hat{\mathbf{w}}^{k}(\Theta^{k})),] (7)

where [TeX: \beta] is the learning rate for [TeX: \Theta] . This update allows softly selecting useful auxiliary tasks (meta-paths) and balance them with the primary task to improve the performance of the primary task. Without balancing tasks with the weighting function [TeX: \mathcal{V}(\cdot;\Theta)] , auxiliary tasks can dominate training and degrade the performance of the primary task.
The model parameters [TeX: \mathbf{w}^{k}] for tasks can be updated with optimized [TeX: \Theta^{k+1}] in (7) as
[TeX: \displaystyle\mathbf{w}^{k+1}=\mathbf{w}^{k}-\alpha\nabla_{\mathbf{w}}\mathcal{L}^{pr+au}(\mathbf{w}^{k};\Theta^{k+1}).] (8)

Remarks. The proposed formulation can suffer from the meta-overfitting [57, 58] meaning that the parameters [TeX: \Theta] to learn weights for softly selecting meta-paths and balancing the tasks with the primary task can overfit to the small meta-dataset. In our experiment, we found that the overfitting can be alleviated by meta-validation sets [57]. To learn [TeX: \Theta] that is generalizable across meta-training sets, we optimize [TeX: \Theta] across [TeX: k] different meta-datasets like [TeX: k] -fold cross validation using the following equation:

[TeX: \displaystyle\Theta^{k+1}\;=\;\underset{D^{pr(meta)}\sim CV\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;}{\Theta^{k}\;-\;\;\beta\;\;\mathbb{E}\left[\;\nabla_{\Theta}\mathcal{L}^{pr}(\hat{\mathbf{w}}^{k}(\Theta^{k}))\;\right],}] (9)

where [TeX: D^{pr(meta)}\sim CV] is a meta-dataset from cross validation. We used 3-fold cross validation and the gradients of [TeX: \Theta] w.r.t different meta-datasets are averaged to update [TeX: \Theta^{k}] , see Algorithm 1. The cross validation is crucial to alleviate meta-overfitting and more discussion is Section V-B.
